title: My Brother's Great Invention
hook: A boy's simple idea changes his family's life — can ordinary kids invent too?

characters.name: Rohit
characters.role: The inventor, a curious Class 7 student who loves solving problems

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Rohit's sister, his biggest supporter and tester

characters.name: Amma
characters.role: Their mother, who inspires Rohit with her daily struggles

slides.title: My Brother's Great Invention
slides.storyContext: An ordinary boy, an ordinary problem, and an extraordinary idea.

slides.title: The Problem That Started It All
slides.storyContext: Rohit watched his mother struggle every morning. During the monsoon, wet clothes took forever to dry in their Mumbai apartment. No balcony, no sunlight, no space. One day, sitting on the kitchen floor with a cup of chai, Rohit asked: 'Amma, what if we didn't have to wait for the sun?' That single question began his invention journey.
slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes the best inventions start when someone notices a real problem in their own home.

slides.title: What Makes a Good Invention?

points.label: Solves a Real Problem
points.text: Rohit's invention wasn't fancy or new — it solved something his family faced daily.

points.label: Uses Simple Materials
points.text: He didn't need expensive equipment. Just plastic pipes, an old fan, and some clever thinking.

points.label: Helps Many People
points.text: When Priya heard about it, she told their neighbours. Soon, three families wanted one.

slides.inSimpleWords: A great invention doesn't have to be complicated. It just has to make life easier.

image.alt: What Makes a Good Invention? — My Brother's Great Invention

slides.title: The Story's Main Characters

points.label: Rohit
points.text: Not a genius. Just observant, patient, and stubborn enough to keep trying when his first attempt failed.

points.label: Priya
points.text: She doesn't invent, but she believes in him and helps test the machine. Every inventor needs someone like Priya.

points.label: Amma
points.text: She doesn't directly help, but her problem was the spark. Sometimes the best inspiration comes from watching someone you love struggle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story has characters we recognize — the doer, the believer, and the one who inspires.

slides.title: The Theme: Turning Everyday Problems Into Opportunities

points.label: Observation
points.text: Rohit wasn't looking for a big problem. He noticed something small that annoyed his mother.

points.label: Curiosity
points.text: Instead of accepting 'that's just how it is,' he asked 'what if?' — the most powerful words for inventors.

points.label: Persistence
points.text: His first version didn't work. His second didn't work either. But he kept going.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inventors aren't born. They're made when someone refuses to accept 'that's impossible.'

slides.title: Important Vocabulary from the Story

points.label: Invention
points.text: A new device or process created to solve a problem or make something better.

points.label: Innovation
points.text: The act of introducing something new, or a new idea applied to something old.

points.label: Prototype
points.text: The first working model of an invention, often rough and improved later.

points.label: Perseverance
points.text: The quality of continuing despite difficulties — Rohit's greatest strength.

slides.inSimpleWords: These words describe what happens when someone decides to change the world, one small fix at a time.

slides.title: Rohit's First Prototype
slides.storyContext: Rohit took an old table fan (₹200 from the market), three plastic pipes from the plumber, and a wooden frame. He built a drying chamber that forces warm air over wet clothes. It took him two weeks. The first version was loud and smelly. But it worked.

example.problem: The clothes took 3–4 hours to dry naturally. Rohit wanted to reduce it to 1 hour using a fan and air circulation.
example.solution: He arranged pipes in a box so that hot air from the fan flows across the wet clothes hanging inside. After two failures, he added a thermometer to prevent overheating. Cost: ₹250. Time: 1 hour. Success: Yes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even simple ideas need testing, failing, and trying again.

image.alt: Rohit's First Prototype — My Brother's Great Invention

slides.title: What Would You Invent?
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. Think about your own home or your school. What's something that wastes time, creates mess, or makes someone's life harder? What small change could fix it?

example.problem: A student notices that their little sister loses her pencils every day. What simple invention could help her remember where they are?
example.solution: A pencil holder attached to her desk with a bell inside. When someone picks up a pencil, the bell rings. Cost: ₹50. Simple but effective — just like Rohit's idea.

slides.inSimpleWords: You don't need to invent flying cars. Start small. Fix one thing in your home or school today.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Rohit's story teaches us that inventions don't come from labs only — they come from kitchens, from watching our mothers, from asking 'what if?'
The best inventions solve real problems using simple ideas and materials.
Every inventor fails first. Failure is part of the journey, not the end of it.
You don't need to be a genius to invent. You need curiosity, observation, and the courage to try.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rohit teaches us that we are all capable of inventing, innovating, and changing our world.
